title: Ukraine’s Crimean Bridge attack is a very personal humiliation for Putin
author: Peter Dickinson
text:
Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge in spectacular fashion early on November 17, destroying the central road section and main arch of this strategically important structure linking occupied Crimea to Russia. Ukraine’s groundbreaking attack has significant military implications, while also dealing a powerful symbolic blow to Russian President Vladimir Putin as he prepares to meet the US and Chinese leaders later this week.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed the strike as an “unprecedented operation” that had been underway for several weeks. According to Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian military initially focused on methodically eroding Russian air defense capabilities close to the bridge, before launching a combined missile and drone assault early on Tuesday morning using a range of domestically produced weapons systems.

The results were stunning. Within hours, images of the partially destroyed bridge were flooding social media. Celebratory memes soon followed as Ukrainians cheered a very welcome victory amid the relentless Russian bombardment of Ukraine’s cities and critical infrastructure. Zelenskyy framed the Crimean Bridge attack as a direct response to Russia’s civilian bombing campaign. “Ukraine’s defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so,” he commented. “We will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered.”

The damage done to the Crimean Bridge is extensive. The destroyed section featured the main arch of the bridge’s road traffic span and was raised to allow merchant shipping to pass beneath. It is not clear whether debris from the collapsed section will now create a maritime bottleneck. Repairing the bridge would likely require multiple cranes and barges, which would be extremely challenging in the current wartime conditions. It is therefore likely that reconstruction works will have to wait until a peace deal is signed.

Ukraine’s attack will have significant implications for the Russian occupation of Crimea and the ongoing invasion. With the road over the bridge now out of action, resupplying the occupied Ukrainian peninsula from Russia will become much more difficult. This will also impact the supply logistics of the Russian army in southern Ukraine. While the rail span of the bridge remains operational, it has long been subject to restrictions due to damage sustained during an earlier Ukrainian strike.

With the Crimean Bridge no longer open to traffic, military and civilian vehicles seeking to travel between Crimea and Russia will be forced to use the land bridge that passes through occupied southern Ukraine. Over the past year, this route has come under the fire control of Ukraine’s mid-range strike drones, leading some to dub it “the highway of death.” It is not a journey that many will relish.

This week’s successful Crimean Bridge operation underlines Ukraine’s growing military strength. When Russia’s full-scale invasion began almost five years ago, Kyiv barely had any long-range strike capabilities. The Ukrainian military now possesses an array of powerful domestically produced weapons and is evidently able to strike high-value targets. The Crimean Bridge was one of the most heavily defended infrastructure sites under Russian control. Ukraine’s ability to penetrate the bridge’s extensive layered air defenses will have set off alarm bells in the Kremlin.

While the practical consequences of Ukraine’s strike on the Crimean Bridge should not be underestimated, the symbolic value of the attack arguably outweighs everything else. For Putin, the partial destruction of the Crimean Bridge is a personal humiliation that ranks alongside his worst moments of the entire war.

This attack is particularly embarrassing for Putin because he is so closely associated with the seizure of Crimea. Ever since Russian troops took control of the Ukrainian peninsula in spring 2014, the capture of Crimea has been central to the personality cult surrounding Putin. When the Crimean Bridge was unveiled four years later, Putin was the first to officially drive across the structure amid much fanfare. Overnight, the bridge became a symbol of Russia’s claim to Crimea and Putin’s determination to retain control over the occupied peninsula.

From Putin’s perspective, the timing of Ukraine’s attack could hardly be worse. In two days, he is due to sit down with his American and Chinese counterparts for a landmark trilateral meeting that was supposed to underline Russia’s status as a leading global power. Instead, Putin will approach this week’s summit in China with global attention fixed firmly on his faltering Ukraine invasion. Russia’s inability to defend key infrastructure against Ukrainian airstrikes makes a mockery of Putin’s claims to military superpower status and will cast a long shadow over his geopolitical posturing in Shenzhen.

When Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, he vowed to demilitarize Ukraine. Nearly five years later, Ukraine is now one of Europe’s most formidable military powers and has emerged as a global leader in drone warfare. Nothing captures Putin’s failure quite as poetically as the destruction of the bridge he built to celebrate his Crimean conquest and cement his place in Russian history.

Peter Dickinson is editor of the Atlantic Council’s UkraineAlert service.
